# codeblast

codeblast is a deterministic code graph CLI that tells a developer or an AI agent what breaks before a change is merged.

## What it is

codeblast parses a repository with the TypeScript compiler API (function level) and the Python stdlib
AST (file level, with typed-call upgrades) into a single-file SQLite graph in which every node and every
edge carries the `file:line` where the dependency actually occurs. It then projects that one graph three
ways: `impact` answers "what breaks if I change this symbol", split into direct callers, transitive
dependents and affected test files; `change` answers "what did this PR structurally change" as symbols
and dependency edges added, removed or renamed between two git refs; `archmap` answers "what does this
project look like" as an interactive HTML map with module to file to symbol drill-down, symbol links
into source lines and circular-dependency detection. No language model decides node membership or edge
existence — an LLM is used for exactly one job, giving clustered modules human-readable names. The same
graph serves two front ends: humans read the CLI, the HTML maps and an optional PR comment bot; AI
agents read the `--json` outputs through the contract in SKILL.md.

## Install

```bash
npx codeblast demo            # build a graph of the current repo, run one impact query, emit the map
npm i -g codeblast            # or install globally
npx skills add alloevil/codeblast   # install as an agent skill
```

Requirements, from `package.json` and SKILL.md: Node >= 22.13.0 (for built-in SQLite) or Bun, plus
`python3` if the target repo contains Python. The target repository's own dependencies must be
installed — a missing `node_modules` turns external calls into blind spots. Current version is 0.3.0,
licensed MIT.

## Quickstart

```bash
# 1. Build the graph (required first; re-runs only reprocess files whose content hash changed)
codeblast index <repo-root> --db graph.db

# 2. Blast radius of a symbol, before you touch it
codeblast impact graph.db "createFlatProxy" --json

# 3. Structural diff of a change you already made
codeblast change <repo-root> HEAD~1 HEAD --json

# 4. Interactive architecture map
codeblast archmap graph.db --out arch.html --repo-url https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>

# 5. Optional: git co-change coupling, for edges static analysis cannot see
codeblast cochange <repo-root> graph.db
```

`codeblast index` prints one JSON object including `files_indexed`, `nodes`, `edges`, `blind_spots` and
`failures`; a non-zero exit with `failures > 0` means the graph is incomplete and must not be queried.
For CI, copy `.github/workflows-template/codeblast.yml` into the target repo: it runs
`npx codeblast pr-comment` and posts a sticky comment only when stdout is non-empty.

## Verifiable claims

Machine-readable versions of all of these, with metric, method, repro command and evidence path, are at
https://alloevil.github.io/codeblast/claims.json.

1. **tRPC impact recall 28/28 (100%).** 30 mutants were injected one at a time into test-covered
   TypeScript functions of trpc/trpc; the full vitest suite was run per mutant to get the ground-truth
   set of failing test files, and recall counts a mutant as a hit only when the predicted affected-test
   set contains all of them. 2 of the 30 mutants were not killed by the suite (dead code path or
   type-only) and are excluded. Repro:
   `bash eval/setup_benchmarks.sh && python3 eval/mutation_check.py /tmp/trpc /tmp/trpc-full.db 30`.
   Evidence: https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/eval/mutation-2026-08-28-trpc-n30.json
2. **tRPC mean precision 0.358 over the same 28 mutants.** Most predicted affected tests do not fail.
   This is the deliberate cost of preferring false positives to false negatives. Repro: average the
   per-mutant `precision` field of the same file. Evidence: same file as claim 1.
3. **graphql-tools impact recall 10/10 (100%), mean precision 0.331.** Second benchmark repository,
   npm workspaces with babel-jest, run through the same harness with `--runner jest`. Suspected misses
   are re-run on restored source; a test that still fails without the mutation is judged flaky and
   removed from the ground truth. Repro:
   `python3 eval/mutation_check.py /tmp/graphql-tools /tmp/graphql-tools.db 10 --runner jest`.
   Evidence: https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/eval/mutation-2026-09-07-graphql-tools-n10.json
4. **Call-graph channel mean precision 0.744, with combined recall 15/15.** A 15-mutant tRPC run
   records both channels per mutant: `precision` for the combined call plus import prediction and
   `precision_call` for the call-graph-reachable subset. Evidence:
   https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/eval/mutation-2026-08-31-trpc-n15.json
5. **Call-only prediction: precision 0.702, recall 2/14 (14%).** A controlled channel ablation scored
   the call-only prediction against the same ground truth as the combined one. Dropping the conservative
   import channel buys precision and destroys recall, because tests frequently reach the target from
   inside anonymous callbacks the call graph cannot see. This is why the `file` channel exists and why
   SKILL.md forbids agents from discarding it. Evidence:
   https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/eval/mutation-2026-08-28-trpc-n15-channel.json
6. **PR bot silence: 42 of 50 real commits produced no comment, 50 of 50 runs completed.**
   `eval/pr_replay.py` walked 50 consecutive non-merge commits of trpc/trpc and ran `pr-comment` on each
   against its parent. Repro: `python3 eval/pr_replay.py 0 /tmp/pr-replay`. Evidence:
   https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/eval/pr-replay-2026-08-28-trpc-n50.json
7. **PR comment usefulness under independent blind review: 25%, then 75%, then 57%, then 20%.**
   Four review rounds are logged in intent.md (2/8, 9/12, 4/7, 1/5). The 87.5% figure that appears in
   older project text is the authoring agent rating its own eight comments; intent.md keeps both numbers
   side by side and treats the gap as measured evidence of reviewer bias. Treat 57-75% as the optimistic
   band and 20-25% as the pessimistic one; the reviewed comment bodies are committed under
   `eval/pr-replay-2026-08-28-window2/` (12 comments) and `eval/pr-replay-2026-08-28-window3/`
   (7 comments) so the rating can be redone. Evidence:
   https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/intent.md
8. **The 100% recall promise is a CI gate, not a slogan.** The weekly `acceptance` workflow indexes both
   benchmark repositories, asserts graph scale (tRPC over 900 files and over 15000 edges; graphql-tools
   over 300 files and over 8000 edges) as a sentinel against silent file loss, then fails the run and
   opens an issue labelled `acceptance-regression` if mutation recall is not 100%. Evidence:
   https://github.com/alloevil/codeblast/blob/main/.github/workflows/acceptance.yml

9. **tRPC graph scale — 957 files, 6248 nodes, 17072 edges, 0 failures.** One `codeblast index` run of
   published 0.3.0 against trpc/trpc at commit `66d0544`. Deterministic for a given commit and version;
   the commit is part of the claim because counts drift with upstream. `blind_spots` was 14725 — that
   counts unresolved and dynamic references and is expected to be large on a real TypeScript monorepo, so
   graph health is judged by `failures`, not by `blind_spots`. Wall-clock time is machine-dependent and
   is not claimed. Repro:
   `git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/trpc/trpc.git && git -C trpc checkout 66d0544 && npx codeblast@0.3.0 index ./trpc --db /tmp/graph.db`

Numbers deliberately not claimed here: the co-change pair count and the unit-test count. Note that the
showcase page reports 5.9k nodes for tRPC against the 6248 measured above; both are real runs against
different upstream commits, which is why any node or edge count is only meaningful with a commit attached.

## When to use it

- You are about to change an exported TypeScript symbol in a monorepo and want the callsite list and the
  test list before you edit, not after CI fails.
- You are an AI agent editing code and need the affected symbols in context so a rename or signature
  change does not silently miss a call site; `impact --json` before the edit, `change --json` after it.
- You are reviewing a PR and want the structural delta (edges added, symbols renamed, new symbols with
  no test coverage) separated from formatting noise.
- You have just inherited an unfamiliar TypeScript or Python repository and want a navigable map whose
  every box and arrow can be opened at the source line that justifies it.
- You need the answer to be checkable by someone who does not trust the tool, because every claim
  carries `file:line`.

## When NOT to use it

- **You want function-level guarantees on Python.** Python support is file level with typed-call
  upgrades. Duck typing and dynamic dispatch make a zero-miss promise impossible in principle and the
  project refuses to pretend otherwise.
- **You want a small, precise impact list.** Mean precision is 0.33-0.36 overall (about 0.70-0.92 on the
  call channel). The engine over-approximates on purpose; an interface method call fans out to every
  implementer. Read the `call` channel first and treat the full list as the test set.
- **Your dependency graph runs through things static analysis cannot resolve** — dynamic `require`,
  `eval`, subprocess boundaries, uninstalled dependencies, test-framework globals. These are recorded in
  `blind_spots` with an explicit "impact may be underestimated" warning rather than dropped, but a
  repository dominated by them will get a thin graph.
- **You want a presentation diagram or a collaborative canvas.** `archmap` emits facts for navigation.
  Rendering a pretty picture is out of scope; feed the JSON to a diagram tool instead.
- **You want cross-service or cross-repository edges, or Java support.** The graph model reserves the
  node types but v1 does not populate those edges, and Java is explicitly not implemented.
- **You want the PR bot to be a review substitute.** Independent blind review put comment usefulness
  between 20% and 75% depending on the round and the rater's criteria. It is a structural-change signal,
  not a reviewer.

## Compared to LLM-generated diagram tools

The comparison the repository actually makes is a mechanism comparison, not a feature checklist:

| | How the graph is produced | Can a claim be checked |
|---|---|---|
| LLM diagram tools | a model reads the code and draws a graph | no — the graph is the model's opinion |
| codeblast | `tsc` / Python AST parse produces nodes and edges; an LLM only names modules | yes — every node, edge and conclusion carries `file:line` |

The design record (`intent.md`) states the rule behind this: layer L1, the graph, must be deterministic,
and an LLM is permitted only at layer L2, the folding and naming layer. It cites the failure of
LLM-welded edges as unverifiable as the reason. That same record also fixes what codeblast deliberately
does not try to be: not a general code-retrieval context engine, not a code-health scoring product, not
a collaborative canvas, and not a cross-service graph in v1. Those boundaries are scope decisions taken
by the project; this document makes no claim about how any named third-party product performs.

## FAQ

**What does codeblast actually guarantee?** Within the statically analyzable scope of an in-repo
TypeScript codebase, the predicted set of affected test files is a superset of the tests that really
fail — verified by mutation testing on two independent repositories (trpc/trpc, 28/28 killed mutants;
ardatan/graphql-tools, 10/10) and enforced weekly in CI, which opens an issue if recall drops below
100%. The guarantee is always stated with that scope attached: anything static analysis cannot resolve
is listed as a blind spot, and the project bans unqualified "zero miss" wording.

**Why is precision so low, and is that a bug?** Mean precision is 0.358 on the 28-mutant tRPC run and
0.331 on the 10-mutant graphql-tools run, meaning most predicted affected tests do not fail. It is a
deliberate trade, and it was measured: a controlled ablation that kept only call-graph edges raised
call-channel precision to 0.702 but dropped recall to 2 of 14 killed mutants. A 2026-09-03 attempt to
raise precision by pruning pure re-export barrel files and narrowing interface fan-out was rejected by
the data because it would have caused guaranteed misses, so precision is no longer an optimization
target.

**Does it work on Python?** Yes, at file level, with typed-call upgrades that resolve named-import
calls and simple constructor or annotation-derived method calls. That is enough for the architecture
map and a file-level change map, and `impact` reaches method level in practice, but the zero-miss
promise remains TypeScript-only. The sgp showcase map at
https://alloevil.github.io/codeblast/sgp-arch.html is the Python example, including a detected
circular dependency between `sgp_utils` and `solver_transfer`.

**How do I use it from an AI coding agent?** Install it as a skill with
`npx skills add alloevil/codeblast`, then call `codeblast impact <db> "<symbol>" --json` before editing
and `codeblast change <repo> HEAD~1 HEAD --json` after editing. SKILL.md carries the interpretation
rules that matter: never present the impact list as complete while `blind_spot_count > 0`, never drop
the `file` channel to shorten the list, never claim function-level precision on Python, treat
`truncated: true` as "recommend the full suite", and never report `co_change_hints` as impact.

**Is the PR bot noisy?** By construction it is silent when nothing structural changed: replayed over 50
real tRPC commits it emitted nothing on 42 of them and never failed. Whether the remaining comments are
worth reading is the honest weak point — four rounds of independent blind review scored 25%, 75%, 57%
and 20% useful, with failures concentrated in zero-impact changes to auxiliary directories and in
type-surface changes that older engine versions did not treat as structural. Both classes have since
been addressed and both the ratings and the fixes are logged in intent.md.
